key_insight: Channel geometry alone can strongly tune capillary-driven transport and analyte confinement in paper-based microdevices, with circular channels flowing fastest and diverging-converging channels flowing slowest.
engineering_relevance: Geometry-guided channel design offers a simple, low-cost way to control passive fluid timing and preconcentration in paper diagnostics and other capillary microfluidic platforms.
method: Tested five paper channel geometries: converging-diverging, diverging-converging, wide-to-narrow, circular, and rectangular.
Used geometry-adapted Lucas–Washburn modeling and CFD simulation to predict and compare flow behavior.
Tracked pyrene and benz[α]anthracene under UV to quantify analyte confinement, with cyclodextrin-chitosan coatings to localize retention.
evidence_signal: Experiments showed flow times from 23.1 s (circular) to 65.0 s (diverging-converging), with CFD reproducing the observed velocity distributions and matching geometry-adapted Lucas–Washburn trends.
watch_item: Results are geometry- and surface-coating-dependent, so scaling to other papers, analytes, or fabrication conditions may require re-calibration.
paper_title: Geometry-Driven Passive Fluid Transport in Paper-Based Microdevices
